profile.purpose: Run a side-by-side experiment showing what happens when scrambled eggs are salted 15 minutes before cooking versus during cooking. It is based on Kenji's Ask Kenji column in the New York Times.
profile.thesis: Salting eggs about 15 minutes before scrambling loosens their proteins so the curds hold their moisture. Salting at the end lets liquid weep out onto the surface. Kenji salts in advance but says either is fine depending on the texture you want.
key_takeaways: Salted raw eggs turn a deeper orange and become more translucent as the salt partly dissolves the proteins.
The test is controlled: 200 g of eggs per batch, 1/4 tsp kosher salt, 1/2 tsp vegetable oil, a non-stick pan held at 300° on a Control Freak, and 28 seconds of cooking.
The eggs salted at the last minute released noticeably more liquid when drained for 1 minute than the pre-salted eggs.
Pre-salted eggs did not turn watery or gray, and the curds kept their moisture inside.
Salting up to about 15 minutes ahead is enough; beyond that the returns diminish.
Kenji's routine is to crack and salt the eggs first thing, then make coffee and toast, then cook the eggs.
Kenji encourages viewers to repeat the experiment at home and share their results.

outline.title: Introduction
outline.summary: Kenji explains the video is based on his NYT Ask Kenji column about when to salt scrambled eggs. He notes the article's science explanation is more up to date than the video's.

outline.title: When should I salt my eggs
outline.summary: Kenji frames the common claim that salting early makes eggs watery, runny or gray, mentions his testing in The Food Lab, and sets up the experiment.

outline.title: Salting eggs
outline.summary: Two identical 200 g batches of beaten eggs: one is salted and rested 15 minutes in clear glasses. He explains why the salted eggs turn deeper orange and more translucent as the proteins loosen.

outline.title: Cooking eggs
outline.summary: Both batches are cooked at a controlled 300° for 28 seconds in vegetable oil, the second salted in the pan, then drained for a minute. He compares the liquid released and explains it with a sponge analogy for protein coagulation.

outline.title: Results and recommendation
outline.summary: Kenji compares texture and taste, says neither approach is wrong, and recommends salting up to about 15 minutes ahead. He describes his morning routine and invites viewers to test it themselves.

corrections.note: Kenji warns that the video was recorded before the NYT article's research was finished. The article's explanation of the science is more up to date, though the practical advice in the video is accurate.
After saying the salted eggs' translucency will make a 'big difference' in cooking, he corrects himself: not a big difference, but it does make a difference.
He first says he'll salt the second batch just before it goes into the pan, then changes the plan to salting it while it cooks in the pan.
